newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian Broadcasting Corp Midday Update.
newsitem.headline: Australian Broadcasting Corp Midday Update.

text.p: HOWARD SAYS "TAX DODGERS" WILL BE WORSE OFF UNDER REFORMS
Prime Minister John Howard has given his tax reform agenda a new name, labelling it - LPT - or Lower Personal Tax reform.
Mr Howard has again stressed the overall tax burden will not rise, telling a seniors' meeting in Brisbane, the challenge is to make the tax system better.
Mr Howard said it would be the "tax dodgers" who would be worse off.
The Prime Minister repeated his claim from Wednesday that the drive and thrust of the tax reform was to alter the fundamental mix of the Australian taxation system.
GOVERNMENT TO HONE IN ON TAX LOOPHOLES

The Federal Government says it is seriously committed to closing a number of loopholes which benefit wealthy tax dodgers. The Treasurer has already signalled a tightening of tax concessions like negative gearing and family trusts.
The move could help fund reforms to the taxation system.
The Deputy Prime Minister, Tim Fischer, says the government has already moved swiftly to shut down loopholes surrounding syndicated research and development and infrastructure bonds.
Mr Fischer says he does not care if the clampdown scares wealthy tax payers.
"I'm fed up with those who will drive bulldozers through chinks in the existing tax system, and we want fairness to be very much part of this equation," Mr Fischer said.
APRA TO SEEK PAYMENTS FROM TELSTRA FOR USE OF MUSIC
The Australasian Performing Rights Association says it will be seeking millions of dollars in back payments from Telstra for the use of "music on hold" over the past ten years.
The High Court yesterday upheld a ruling that makes telephone companies liable to pay copyright royalties for the music its customers play when callers are on hold.
APRA and Telstra will soon begin talks to negotiate a settlement and to set licence fees for the music.
APRA said the money raised would be used to create a special fund, which would then be distributed to musicians in Australia and overseas, according to how often their music is played.
GOVERNMENT SEEKS ADVICE ON HIGH COURT KAKADU RULING
The Federal Government is seeking advice from the Attorney-General's office on the implications of the High Court's ruling on mining in Kakadu National Park.
The Court found when the Hawke Government included Coronation Hill in the third stage of Kakadu, resuming the land and not paying any compensation, it breached the Constitution.
The Court ruled that in effect Newcrest Mining still has the right to mine its tenements in Kakadu.
Environment minister Robert Hill and Resources minister Warwick Parer are seeking advice from the Attorney-General, and planning to take a recommendation to Cabinet in the next couple of weeks.

The Federal Government faces the possibility of having to pay tens of millions of dollars in compensation, to prevent Newcrest from exercising its right to mine in the National Park. The area contains one of the world's largest deposits of paladium as well as rich gold deposits.
AUSTRALIA JOINS OTTAWA PROCESS ON LANDMINES
Australia has joined a group of countries trying to fast-track a global ban on landmines.
Australia will now follow a twin-track policy, working inside and oustide the United Nations.

The Foreign Minister, Alexander Downer, announced that Australia will join the so-called Ottawa process, a group of mostly developed states that want to move faster than the larger United Nations Conference on Disarmament.
Australia had been slow to sign-up for the Ottawa group.
Mr Downer said Ottawa was partly feel-good politics because the process outside the UN excludes major land mine countries such as Russia, China, India and Pakistan.
But the Foreign Minister said Australia had already frozen the use of its mines and could offer expertise to the non-UN effort.
AMA OFFERS TO BRIEF GOVERNMENT ON HEROIN TRIAL
The Australian Medical Association has offered to brief the Prime Minister and Coalition MPs on why it now supports a strictly controlled heroin trial in the ACT.
The AMA said it had initially opposed the trial, possibly for the same reasons as Mr Howard.
But President, Dr Keith Woollard, said the AMA dropped its opposition to a scientific study after detailed discussions with the National Centre for Epidemiology and Population Health.
Dr Woollard said the proposed trial was a new approach to substance abuse and addiction which could reduce the high levels of death and disease associated with heroin abuse.

He said if the trail does not produce results it could be abandoned, but if it did not go ahead, the community could be denied a method that could help curb more than 500 deaths a year from heroin abuse.
INVESTIGATORS ON THEIR WAY TO PLANE CRASH SITE IN NT
A team of officers from the Bureau of Air Safety Investigation is expected to arrive at the site of a fatal air crash in the Northern Territory, at lunchtime.
A single-engined Cessna crashed six kilometres south of Katherine, as it approached the town's airport, killing all five people on board.
The charter plane had been travelling from Kununnurra in Western Australia, with four Victorian tourists and a Territory pilot, on board.
The Bureau said the crash was the worst fixed-wing aircraft accident in Australia since the Seaview Air crash in 1994, which killed nine people.
Investigators are expected to be in Katherine for at least two days.
